items.prompt: In what form does light travel through space?

options.label: As a wave
options.feedback: Correct. Light travels as a wave, specifically an electromagnetic wave, which carries energy through empty space.

options.label: As a stream of air
options.feedback: Incorrect. Light does not use air; it travels perfectly well in a vacuum where there is no air at all.

options.label: As a kind of sound
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sound needs a medium like air or water, but light is an electromagnetic wave and does not need any medium.

options.label: As tiny solid balls
options.feedback: Incorrect. Although light has particle-like properties in some situations, it is not made of solid matter; it is energy traveling as waves.

items.ok_line: Light is a wave that needs no medium.
items.ko_line: Light is not air, sound, or solid particles.
items.exp_text: Light is an electromagnetic wave, which means it is a ripple of electric and magnetic fields traveling together through space. Unlike sound or water waves, it does not need air, water, or any other substance to move—it can cross the emptiness of space from the Sun to the Earth.

items.prompt: What is the speed of light in empty space?

options.label: About 300,000 kilometres per hour
options.feedback: Incorrect. That would be too slow by a huge factor; light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second, not per hour.

options.label: About 300,000 kilometres per second
options.feedback: Correct. In a vacuum, light moves at about 300,000 kilometres every second, which is extremely fast.

options.label: About 300,000 metres per second
options.feedback: Incorrect. That is the speed of sound in air, not light; light is about a million times faster, measured in kilometres per second.

options.label: About 3,000 kilometres per second
options.feedback: Incorrect. That is far too slow; the actual value is about 100 times larger, namely 300,000 kilometres per second.

items.ok_line: Light's speed in a vacuum is about 300,000 km/s.
items.ko_line: It is per second, not per hour, and in kilometres, not metres.
items.exp_text: In empty space, light travels at a constant speed of about 300,000 kilometres per second. This value is a fundamental constant of nature, meaning it does not change regardless of the source or the observer. It is so fast that light can circle the Earth more than seven times in one second.

items.prompt: What happens to the speed of light when it moves from air into water?

options.label: It stays the same
options.feedback: Incorrect. The speed of light changes when it enters a denser medium; it slows down in water compared to air.

options.label: It speeds up
options.feedback: Incorrect. Light slows down when moving from air into water because water is denser and interacts more with the wave.

options.label: It slows down
options.feedback: Correct. Light travels slower in water than in air, which is why it bends when entering water at an angle.

options.label: It stops completely
options.feedback: Incorrect. Light does not stop in water; it continues moving, just at a lower speed than in air.

items.ok_line: Light slows down as it enters water.
items.ko_line: It changes speed, not staying, speeding, or stopping.
items.exp_text: When light passes from air into water, it slows down because water is more dense and the electromagnetic wave interacts more with the atoms. This change in speed is what causes the light to bend, or refract, when it hits the surface at an angle—that is why a straw in a glass of water looks broken.

items.prompt: What is a light-year a measure of?

options.label: A unit of time, like a year
options.feedback: Incorrect. Despite the word 'year', a light-year is not a time; it is a distance that light covers in one year.

options.label: A unit of brightness
options.feedback: Incorrect. Brightness is about how much light something gives off, not a distance; a light-year has nothing to do with brightness.

options.label: A unit of speed
options.feedback: Incorrect. Speed is how fast something moves, like kilometres per hour; a light-year is a fixed distance, not a rate.

options.label: A unit of distance
options.feedback: Correct. A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, used to measure vast interstellar and intergalactic distances.

items.ok_line: A light-year is a distance, not time.
items.ko_line: It is about how far light goes in a year.
items.exp_text: A light-year is the distance that light, moving at about 300,000 kilometres per second, covers in one full year. That distance is roughly 9.5 trillion kilometres. Astronomers use it to talk about the enormous gaps between stars and galaxies, because ordinary units like kilometres would become unwieldy.

items.prompt: Why does light from a distant star take a long time to reach us?

options.label: Because the star is extremely far away
options.feedback: Correct. The star is so far that even at light's immense speed, the journey takes many years.

options.label: Because light travels slowly in space
options.feedback: Incorrect. Light travels at its fastest in space; it is not slow, the distances are simply enormous.

options.label: Because the light gets tired along the way
options.feedback: Incorrect. Light does not get tired or slow down; it keeps a constant speed in a vacuum.

options.label: Because the star is very dim
options.feedback: Incorrect. A star's brightness does not affect the travel time; a dim star's light still moves at the same speed.

items.ok_line: Stars are so far that light takes years to arrive.
items.ko_line: It is distance, not low speed or dimness.
items.exp_text: Space is unimaginably huge, and even the nearest star outside our Sun is over four light-years away. Since light has a fixed speed, the only reason its journey takes a long time is the sheer distance. When you see a star tonight, you are seeing light that left that star years ago.

items.prompt: What does the finite speed of light imply about seeing distant objects?

options.label: We see them exactly as they are right now
options.feedback: Incorrect. Because light takes time to travel, we see them as they were in the past, not as they are now.

options.label: We see them as they were in the past
options.feedback: Correct. Since light takes time to reach us, the image we see is always a little old, more so for faraway objects.

options.label: We see them only if they are moving
options.feedback: Incorrect. Motion is not required; any object that reflects or emits light can be seen, regardless of movement.

options.label: We see them only at night
options.feedback: Incorrect. The time of day does not affect the speed of light; it affects whether the object is illuminated for us.

items.ok_line: We always see objects as they were earlier.
items.ko_line: Light's travel time means we see the past.
items.exp_text: Because light has a finite speed, the information about an object reaches your eye after a delay. For everyday objects like a chair, the delay is tiny, but for the Moon it is over a second, and for a galaxy it can be millions of years. So when you look out into space, you are looking back in time.

items.prompt: What is the main reason that nothing with mass can travel at the speed of light?

options.label: It would be too heavy to move
options.feedback: Incorrect. It is not about weight; the rule comes from the physics of energy and motion, not from practical weight.

options.label: It would melt from friction
options.feedback: Incorrect. Friction is not the reason; in empty space there is no such thing to stop a moving object.

options.label: It would need infinite energy to reach that speed
options.feedback: Correct. As an object with mass speeds up, it needs more and more energy, and reaching light speed would require infinite energy.

options.label: It would get lost in space
options.feedback: Incorrect. Getting lost is not a physical reason; the limitation is about energy, not navigation.

items.ok_line: Mass needs infinite energy to hit light speed.
items.ko_line: It is a fundamental limit, not friction or weight.
items.exp_text: According to the theory of relativity, as a massive object accelerates, its mass effectively increases and the energy needed to keep accelerating grows without bound. To actually reach the speed of light would require an infinite amount of energy, which is impossible. Only massless particles like photons can naturally travel at that speed.

items.prompt: Why does thunder arrive after the lightning that caused it?

options.label: Because sound is faster than light
options.feedback: Incorrect. Light is much faster than sound; that is why the flash arrives first.

options.label: Because the thunder is farther away
options.feedback: Incorrect. Thunder and lightning happen at the same place; the difference is in how fast they travel, not distance.

options.label: Because light is delayed by the storm
options.feedback: Incorrect. Light is not delayed by the storm; it simply travels faster than sound.

options.label: Because sound is slower than light
options.feedback: Correct. Light reaches you almost instantly, while sound takes about three seconds per kilometre, so thunder lags behind.

items.ok_line: Sound travels slower than light, so thunder is late.
items.ko_line: It is because light outruns sound, not the reverse.
items.exp_text: Light travels about a million times faster than sound in air. When lightning strikes, the light reaches your eyes almost immediately, but the sound of thunder has to travel at about 340 metres per second, so it arrives noticeably later. Counting the seconds between the flash and the thunder tells you how far away the lightning is.

items.prompt: What does it mean to say that the speed of light is constant?

options.label: It is the same in every material
options.feedback: Incorrect. Light slows down in materials like glass or water; it is constant only in a vacuum.

options.label: It is the same for every observer in empty space
options.feedback: Correct. In a vacuum, everyone measures the same speed for light, no matter how they are moving.

options.label: It is the same only for stationary objects
options.feedback: Incorrect. Even if you move toward or away from a light source, you still measure the same speed in a vacuum.

options.label: It is the same for all colours of light
options.feedback: Incorrect. All colours travel at the same speed in a vacuum, but that is not what 'constant' means here; it means independent of the observer.

items.ok_line: Light's speed in a vacuum is the same for everyone.
items.ko_line: It does not depend on motion or material, except in a vacuum.
items.exp_text: The constancy of the speed of light is a cornerstone of physics: in empty space, any observer—whether moving toward a light source or away from it—measures exactly the same speed, about 300,000 kilometres per second. This is different from everyday objects, whose speeds add up depending on how you move. In a material like water, however, light does slow down.

items.prompt: What is the best description of a photon?

options.label: A tiny packet of light energy
options.feedback: Correct. A photon is the smallest unit of light, carrying a specific amount of energy that depends on its colour.

options.label: A particle of air that carries light
options.feedback: Incorrect. Photons are not made of air; they are pure energy and can travel through a vacuum.

options.label: A wave that has no energy
options.feedback: Incorrect. Photons have energy; higher frequency light means each photon has more energy.

options.label: A kind of atom
options.feedback: Incorrect. Photons are not atoms; they have no mass and are not made of protons, neutrons, or electrons.

items.ok_line: A photon is a packet of light energy.
items.ko_line: It is energy, not air, wave without energy, or an atom.
items.exp_text: A photon is the fundamental particle of light, a tiny bundle of electromagnetic energy. Each photon has an energy that is directly tied to its colour—blue photons have more energy than red ones. Photons always travel at the speed of light in a vacuum and have no mass, which is why they can move at that speed.
